prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, and its realisation at a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a single two-person part. Reading all eight first-round statements, the committee has sorted itself into two camps of four, and both camps name the other candidate as their alternative. That tells me the real question is the one the chair put: does breadth and novelty (B022) outweigh a settled, tightly attributed invention (B012)? On the criterion I quoted in my March 2026 lecture, a discovery or invention and the people responsible for the original work, B012 answers cleanly. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a specific, original idea that makes the lattice trap perturb both clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held Doppler- and recoil-free. Ye's group then took strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime through ultrastable lasers and systematics control. The performance is reproduced by several laboratories and by comparisons between institutes, and it has already been used for millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and relativistic geodesy. As to the chair's question on citation wording, I would word it around the lattice-clock architecture, as Kroll and Lindroth propose, so that trapped-ion, comb and other lattice-clock contributors are not implicitly demoted. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb, which makes optical clocks countable, not this step. I regard the pending SI redefinition as consequence and not criterion: the demonstrated performance is what the prize would recognise.
statement.case_against: Credit for the clock regime is wider than two names. Ion-clock groups at NIST and PTB, SYRTE, and the JILA team members around Ye contributed to the 10^-18 milestone, and Johansson is right that priority for the magic-wavelength idea over contemporaneous proposals has not been verified from the material I have. A pair necessarily draws a line that some in the community will contest. The prize is also an instrument-and-precision achievement, and several colleagues weigh that below the opening of a new regime of quantum matter. B022 has the broadest opening support, a clear prediction-then-observation arc, and phenomenology that every member accepts is reproduced. My own ranking of it second is sincere. If the committee could show that the 2018 experimental authorship and Dean's hBN-device contribution fit within the named experimental credit, my reservation about it would shrink to youth and the unresolved mechanism, and I could not rule out changing my vote.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that B022 is a discovery found by listening to nature after a sharp prediction, that the core phenomenology is robust and the open mechanism is a follow-up question, and that the field's age does not justify delay.
responses.response: I accept that the existence of the flat-band-driven correlated insulators and superconducting domes is not in doubt, and I agree that a citation limited to what was predicted and observed avoids the mechanism problem. Our disagreement is narrower than the first-round ranking suggests. You concede yourself that the 2018 experimental breakthrough was a group effort and that Dean's devices and other early work lie outside the three names. That is not a technicality to me. In my own field, a discovery that depends on how a device is made, in this case twist-angle control and hBN encapsulation, is hard to credit to one laboratory after the fact, and the committee asks who is responsible for the original work. For the clock the record is short enough to state in two names. I also do not accept that a measurement is a lesser class of finding. A new regime of measurement that reveals what could not be tested before is a discovery in the same sense.

responses.point: Mehlig answered my first-round remark by saying that shared experimental credit is common in modern materials experiments, that the prize can recognise the group leader and name the discovery, and that the citation should lean on transport and device evidence, not only on theory.
responses.response: I agree that shared credit is normal and that a prize can name a leader. My worry is different. In most materials experiments the leader is clearly identifiable. Here the chair has asked us to verify the author record of the 2018 papers, which includes the first author, and the committee cannot do that within this stage. I welcome your point that the citation should rest on the transport and device evidence, since that is exactly what makes the claim secure. But it also brings Dean, Young, Yacoby, Efetov and Yazdani closer to the centre of the discovery, not further from it. If the committee sets that aside as a limit of the three-person rule, I understand the logic, but I would then prefer the configuration that does not need the exception.

responses.point: Eriksson warns that the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gives flat bands but does not predict the correlated phases, and concedes that waiting a few years would settle both interpretation and credit.
responses.response: This is the most useful caution in the round. If the theory side is restricted to what it did predict, the flat band at the magic angle, then the B022 citation is honest, but the claim that theory anticipated a new phase of matter is weaker than the opening ballots implied. Your own concession that waiting would settle the mechanism and the credit is a point I share, and it makes the maturity gap with B012 concrete. I do not think the clock needs that wait, because performance, replication and interpretation are settled now. I would also say that a prize for the flat-band prediction and the first observation is a perfectly defensible prize, just a few years from being as secure as this one.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B022 on the grounds that seven of eight members rank it in the top three and that all eight proposed the same three names, and he asks that the author record of the first reports be examined before the vote.
responses.response: I agree with your request for that examination, and I thank you for moving off IceCube for the reasons you gave, which match my own about source identification. I would add that agreement on three names is partly an artefact of the supplied credit string. Four of the eight of us flagged Dean's group and the first author as outside it, so shared proposals do not show that attribution is uncontested. I also want to be careful about support counts, which should not decide this. On your question about a combined configuration, I have looked for a fair two-part split and have not found one: it would pair one moire name with Katori and Ye, and there is no non-arbitrary choice among the three B022 names, which I think is a reason to prefer a single part.

uncertainties: Whether the author and credit record of the 2018 B022 papers, including Dean's group and the first author, can be verified well enough to bring B022 within three names. If it can, I would reconsider.
Whether priority for the magic-wavelength proposal over contemporaneous proposals, and the weight of ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups, is as clean as I recall. I cannot verify it here.
Whether colleagues who rank B012 low accept metrology as a prize-level discovery after the 2005 comb prize, and how the committee weighs cleaner attribution against breadth.
The timing of the SI redefinition of the second, which I treat as consequence and not criterion.
statement.conflict_note: No documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. I hold a University of Tokyo fellowship and a JSPS fellowship and have long-running exchanges with Japanese universities, where Katori works, so I repeat that disclosure and would accept recusal guidance from the chair if the committee judges it relevant. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but he is not a credited name on any shortlisted part, and I have no connection to the B022 names.
